The inflated multinomial logit

Benjamin E. Bagozzi

Source: vignettes/inflation.Rmd
inflation.Rmd

Two kinds of abstainers

In a model of vote choice the base alternative, abstention, holds two kinds of people: routine nonvoters, who would not have voted whatever the campaign did, and occasional nonvoters, who weighed the candidates and stayed home this time. A standard multinomial logit treats them as one group and, when the mixture is real, misstates how the covariates move people between abstention and the candidates. The baseline-inflated multinomial logit (BIMNL) of Bagozzi and Marchetti (2017) adds a split equation that sorts cases into a regime where the base alternative is observed with certainty and a regime where the multinomial choice operates:

P(si=1∣zi)=ϕi=F(zi′δ),P(yi=b)=(1−ϕi)+ϕiPib,P(yi=j)=ϕiPij(j≠b), P(s_i = 1 \mid z_i) = \phi_i = F(z_i'\delta), \qquad P(y_i = b) = (1 - \phi_i) + \phi_i P_{ib}, \qquad P(y_i = j) = \phi_i P_{ij} \ (j \ne b),

with FF logistic (the default) or standard normal and PijP_{ij} the multinomial logit probabilities. The same structure fits any alternative that mixes two populations: inflate names it (default: the base).

In the discrete-choice literature, with the logistic split equation this is the parametrized logit captivity model of Swait and Ben-Akiva (1987) with captivity to the inflated alternative only. Their model generalizes the dogit of Gaudry and Dagenais (1979), which adds to the multinomial logit a share of decision makers who are captive to an alternative, by letting the captivity odds depend on covariates. Here the captives of the inflated alternative are the routine nonvoters, their share is 1−ϕi1 - \phi_i, and their odds are θi=(1−ϕi)/ϕi=e−zi′δ\theta_i = (1 - \phi_i)/\phi_i = e^{-z_i'\delta}.

Fitting the model

The formula has two parts: the outcome equation and, after |, the split equation. imnl() fits by maximum likelihood with a multistart because the mixture likelihood can have several local maxima (see below).

library(polychoice)
data(pa2006)
f <- vote ~ canvass + phone + democrat + republican + canvass:democrat + canvass:republican +
  phone:democrat + phone:republican + household + age + female + voted2004 + district156
m0 <- mnl(f, data = pa2006)
m1 <- imnl(vote ~ canvass + phone + democrat + republican + canvass:democrat +
             canvass:republican + phone:democrat + phone:republican + household + age +
             female + voted2004 + district156 |
             household + age + female + voted2004 + district156, data = pa2006)
summary(m1)
#> Inflated multinomial logit (inflated alternative: abstain, logit split) 
#> Call: imnl(formula = vote ~ canvass + phone + democrat + republican + 
#>     canvass:democrat + canvass:republican + phone:democrat +

The summary shows the outcome equations (alternative:term), the split equation (infl_term, the coefficients of zi′δz_i'\delta on the scale of the link), the observed share of the inflated alternative, and the mean fitted probability of the choice regime. The sign convention of the split equation: δ\delta models P(si=1)P(s_i = 1), the probability of being in the choice regime, so the negative infl_age printed above means that older respondents are less likely to be in the choice regime, that is, more likely to be routine abstainers. The estimates agree with the published Table A.3 of Bagozzi and Marchetti (2017) to within 0.002 in the coefficients and standard errors that the package’s tests compare (for example 1.564 (0.557) for the Republican/other canvassing coefficient against the published 1.566 (0.558); the package’s tests pin a selection of them at tolerances of one to ten percent), and the published log-likelihoods of both models to their two printed decimals.

Is the split equation needed?

The plain multinomial logit is the special case ϕi=1\phi_i = 1, a boundary of the parameter space, so the likelihood-ratio test does not have its usual distribution (and the split-equation slopes are not identified under the null, so no simple correction exists; a split with an intercept only is the exception, below under “Tests for captive choosers”). The literature compares the two models with the Vuong (1989) test, the information criteria, and the classification tables: compare_models() lines up the information criteria, vuong() and classification() give the other two.

compare_models(MNL = m0, BIMNL = m1)
#>  model                                                                    type
#>    MNL                                                       Multinomial logit
#>  BIMNL Inflated multinomial logit (inflated alternative: abstain, logit split)
#>  inflate    n df    loglik      AIC      BIC mcfadden converged boundary
#>          1998 42 -2110.593 4305.187 4540.382    0.160      TRUE    FALSE
#>  abstain 1998 48 -2069.971 4235.942 4504.737    0.176      TRUE    FALSE
#>  ill_conditioned n_modes
#>            FALSE       1
#>            FALSE       2
vuong(m1, m0)
#> Vuong test:  m1 = m1 [ Inflated multinomial logit (inflated alternative: abstain, logit split) ]
#>              m2 = m0 [ Multinomial logit ]
#> positive statistics favor m1
#> 
#>  correction statistic p_m1_better p_m2_better p_two_sided
#>         raw     4.479       0.000       1.000       0.000
#>         AIC     3.817       0.000       1.000       0.000
#>         BIC     1.965       0.025       0.975       0.049
#> Note: The inflated multinomial logit and the multinomial logit are nested at the boundary phi = 1, where the normal reference does not hold for testing the uninflated model; boot_lr_test() calibrates the statistic.

A positive Vuong statistic favours the first model; the three rows apply no correction, the AIC correction, and the BIC correction for the number of parameters. The normal reference of the Vuong test does not hold for models nested at a boundary (Wilson 2015), so the calibrated comparison is the parametric bootstrap under the multinomial logit, boot_lr_test(m0, m1), which refits both models on data simulated from the MNL and reports bootstrap p-values for the likelihood-ratio and Vuong statistics. It is slow: every replicate refits the inflated model with its whole search (about 40 seconds on these data), so the default B = 199 takes more than two hours on one core, and cores spreads the replicates over workers; it is not run here.

Quantities of interest by stage

Predictions can be made for the observed outcome (type = "prob"), for the multinomial stage alone (type = "prob_outcome", the probabilities among cases in the choice regime), and for the regime itself (type = "regime", the probability of being in the choice regime). The labels infl_ and "inflation" (the block of summary(), the component of tidy(), and stage = "inflation" in first_difference()) all mean the split equation.

head(predict(m1, type = "regime"), 3)
#>         1         2         3 
#> 0.9751583 0.9475315 0.8309676
head(predict(m1, type = "prob_outcome"), 3)
#>      abstain   democrat republican_other nonresponse
#> 1 0.75254430 0.02545574        0.1955426  0.02645737
#> 2 0.34433867 0.08146521        0.5134851  0.06071103
#> 3 0.03832782 0.16109000        0.7232341  0.07734805

first_difference() has the same type switch (the change in the observed probabilities, in the outcome-stage probabilities, or in the regime probability) and a stage argument that says through which equations the covariate is allowed to move: both (default), the outcome equation only, or the split equation only. A covariate that appears in both equations, such as age here, can thus be decomposed.

first_difference(m1, "canvass", from = 0, to = 1)
#> First differences: canvass from 0 to 1 at the covariate profile (delta intervals at 95%)
#>       alternative  from    to   diff  lower upper
#>           abstain 0.296 0.261 -0.035 -0.096 0.025
#>          democrat 0.335 0.273 -0.062 -0.147 0.024
#>  republican_other 0.304 0.389  0.085 -0.009 0.180
#>       nonresponse 0.066 0.077  0.011 -0.042 0.065
first_difference(m1, "age", from = 30, to = 60, type = "regime")
#> First differences: age from 30 to 60 at the covariate profile (delta intervals at 95%)
#> Quantity: P(choice regime) 
#>       alternative  from    to   diff  lower  upper
#>  P(choice regime) 0.937 0.832 -0.106 -0.129 -0.083
first_difference(m1, "age", from = 30, to = 60, stage = "outcome")
#> First differences: age from 30 to 60 at the covariate profile (delta intervals at 95%; outcome stage only)
#>       alternative  from    to   diff  lower  upper
#>           abstain 0.628 0.158 -0.470 -0.536 -0.403
#>          democrat 0.143 0.388  0.245  0.203  0.288
#>  republican_other 0.185 0.378  0.193  0.147  0.239
#>       nonresponse 0.045 0.076  0.031  0.011  0.051

Local maxima

Mixture likelihoods are not globally concave. On pa2006 and on pres2004 a search from 200 starts finds two interior maxima of the BIMNL likelihood. The fit screens fourteen starting values and polishes every one of them. It then challenges the incumbent with rescaled split slopes. Each point where these searches end is classified by the rules of the fit-quality flags: a local maximum, a boundary (diverging coefficients, or a split equation that puts every case in one regime), a saddle, or not converged. m1$search lists the distinct points, and the number of distinct local maxima is reported, with a message when there is more than one; the highest found need not be the global maximum. Then crosscheck = TRUE runs the same search under the other split link and polishes the fit under its own link from the rescaled estimates (which about doubles the time), and start probes other basins (a row of m1$search_theta refits that point).

m1$n_modes
#> [1] 2
m1$search
#>      loglik    type reached reported detail
#> 1 -2069.971 maximum       5     TRUE       
#> 2 -2070.990 maximum      12    FALSE

A fit that reports more than one mode is still the highest maximum found; imnl() says so in a message (hidden in this vignette’s output), so that no analysis rests on a lower maximum unknowingly. Changing the split-equation covariates can change the number and location of the maxima.

The second application: the 2004 presidential vote

pres2004 holds the Campbell and Monson (2008) respondents of the 2004 Election Panel Study (Replication II of Bagozzi and Marchetti 2017).

data(pres2004)
f2 <- vote ~ educ + female + black + hispanic + pid7 + bush_values + battleground + south + gmb +
  agegroup + evangelical + evangelical:gmb + catholic + catholic:gmb + other_religion +
  secular + secular:gmb + ideology + mobilization
p0 <- mnl(f2, data = pres2004)
p1 <- imnl(vote ~ educ + female + black + hispanic + pid7 + bush_values + battleground + south +
             gmb + agegroup + evangelical + evangelical:gmb + catholic + catholic:gmb +
             other_religion + secular + secular:gmb + ideology + mobilization |
             educ + agegroup + mobilization + secular, data = pres2004)
compare_models(MNL = p0, BIMNL = p1)
#>  model                                                                    type
#>    MNL                                                       Multinomial logit
#>  BIMNL Inflated multinomial logit (inflated alternative: abstain, logit split)
#>  inflate    n df   loglik      AIC      BIC mcfadden converged boundary
#>          1341 40 -553.500 1187.000 1395.046    0.548      TRUE    FALSE
#>  abstain 1341 45 -545.279 1180.557 1414.610    0.555      TRUE    FALSE
#>  ill_conditioned n_modes
#>            FALSE       1
#>            FALSE       2
vuong(p1, p0)
#> Vuong test:  m1 = p1 [ Inflated multinomial logit (inflated alternative: abstain, logit split) ]
#>              m2 = p0 [ Multinomial logit ]
#> positive statistics favor m1
#> 
#>  correction statistic p_m1_better p_m2_better p_two_sided
#>         raw     1.680       0.047       0.953       0.093
#>         AIC     0.658       0.255       0.745       0.510
#>         BIC    -1.998       0.977       0.023       0.046
#> Note: The inflated multinomial logit and the multinomial logit are nested at the boundary phi = 1, where the normal reference does not hold for testing the uninflated model; boot_lr_test() calibrates the statistic.

The log-likelihoods of the published Table A.4 reproduce: the inflated model’s -545.279 agrees with the published -545.27 when truncated to its printed digits, and a search from 200 starts finds no interior maximum above it. So do its split-equation coefficients and the outcome-stage coefficients the package’s tests check. Two of the search’s starts end higher, at points where the Kerry and Bush coefficients diverge together (the higher at -542.851): the outcome stage predicts 21 abstainers with certainty, and the split equation puts the other 84 in the captive regime. There the likelihood rises towards a supremum at infinity, a separation within the mixture that the multinomial logit’s data do not show (see ?imnl). The multistart does not reach that region, and the published fit is the highest interior maximum. The raw Vuong statistic computed here is 1.68 (positive values favour the first model, the inflated one; two-sided p = 0.09): it leans towards the inflated model without being decisive. Its BIC-corrected version, which charges the inflated model for its extra parameters, is -2.00 and leans the other way, and the information criteria disagree with each other, as in the published analysis, which reports mixed support for inflation in these data. Which row to read: the raw statistic is Vuong’s, the AIC and BIC rows are his corrections for the difference in parameters; but since the multinomial logit is the boundary case of the inflated model, none of them has a valid normal reference here, and boot_lr_test(p0, p1) gives the calibrated p-values.

Tests for captive choosers

Whether the multinomial logit leaves room for routine choosers can be asked before any inflated model is fit. captivity_test() is the score test of the multinomial logit against the dogit with a constant captive share for each alternative, computed from the multinomial logit fit alone: its joint statistic is the Lagrange multiplier test of Tse (1987), and the one-sided statistic for each alternative is added here. The score of a case for alternative jj is 1{yi=j}/Pij−11\{y_i = j\}/P_{ij} - 1: it grows when the cases that chose jj are ones the multinomial logit thought unlikely to, which is what captive choosers produce. Each alternative gets a one-sided z statistic (captive shares cannot be negative), and a joint test follows.

captivity_test(m0)
#> Score test of the multinomial logit against captive choosers (dogit; one-sided z per alternative, joint chi-square) 
#>                       test statistic df p.value
#>           captive: abstain     0.503 NA  0.3075
#>          captive: democrat    -1.376 NA  0.9156
#>  captive: republican_other     1.282 NA  0.0999
#>       captive: nonresponse    -0.038 NA  0.5153
#>                      joint     3.859  4  0.4254

Because the multinomial logit is an ordinary boundary point of the dogit’s captivity parameters, the score test is regular there, unlike the comparison with the inflated fit. Its weights 1/Pij1/P_{ij} make it heavy-tailed when some fitted probabilities are small; boot_pvalue(m0, captivity_test) calibrates it by simulation (not run here). The same weights cost it power, and here it does not reject although the inflated multinomial logit with a constant captive share of abstention, its own alternative, raises the log-likelihood by 10.5 on one parameter. The score of abstention is 37.3, but its expected information (before the coefficients are partialled out) is 10,186, half of it from one respondent whose fitted probability of abstaining is 0.0002 and who did not abstain, and along the captive share the log-likelihood is convex at zero, so the gain lies away from the null, where a local test does not look. A small statistic is no evidence against captivity. The likelihood-ratio form measures the gain itself: it fits the inflated multinomial logit with an intercept-only split for each requested alternative and refers the likelihood ratio to the 50:50 mixture of chi-square(0) and chi-square(1), since a captive share of zero is a regular boundary point when the alternative’s fitted probabilities vary in a way its constants and slopes cannot absorb (otherwise the share is not identified, and the test says so; one refit per alternative):

captivity_test(m0, alternatives = "abstain", type = "lr")
#> Likelihood-ratio test of the multinomial logit against a constant captive share of each alternative (the inflated multinomial logit with an intercept-only split; p-value from the 50:50 mixture of chi-square(0) and chi-square(1)) 
#>              test statistic df  p.value share
#>  captive: abstain    20.951  1 2.36e-06 0.196

A split equation with covariates, as in Replication I, is not of this kind (its slopes are not identified at the boundary), and boot_lr_test() calibrates that comparison.

Several inflated alternatives

inflate can name several alternatives. A case is then either in the choice regime, where the multinomial logit operates, or captive to one of the inflated alternatives, with the regime probabilities given by a multinomial logit in the split covariates: the parametrized logit captivity model with a captive share for each inflated alternative. In vote choice this holds routine nonvoters and party loyalists in one model. Each inflated alternative gets its own split coefficients, infl_<alternative>:<term>, the log-odds of choosing against captivity to that alternative (positive: less captivity).

set.seed(1)
dc <- rmnl(2000, beta = cbind(b = c(0.5, -1, 0.8), c = c(-0.3, 0.6, -0.5), d = c(0.2, 0.4, 0.3)),
           delta = cbind(a = c(1, 0.8), c = c(1.8, -0.7)), inflate = c("a", "c"))
mc <- imnl(y ~ x1 + x2 | z1, data = dc, inflate = c("a", "c"))
summary(mc)$coefficients[grep("^infl_", names(coef(mc))), ]
#>                      Estimate Std. Error   z value     Pr(>|z|)
#> infl_a:(Intercept)  0.7305562 0.18670464  3.912898 9.119505e-05
#> infl_a:z1           0.7072399 0.09649689  7.329147 2.316215e-13
#> infl_c:(Intercept)  1.9608265 0.23896982  8.205331 2.299558e-16
#> infl_c:z1          -0.8044669 0.13505839 -5.956438 2.577953e-09
head(predict(mc, type = "regime"), 3)
#>      choice         a          c
#> 1 0.4083044 0.5747278 0.01696775
#> 2 0.6484533 0.2001526 0.15139415
#> 3 0.3824451 0.6036018 0.01395317

The split coefficients lie within 1.5 standard errors of the values used to simulate them (1 and 0.8 for a, 1.8 and -0.7 for c). The likelihood can also peak near the limit in which the choice regime never picks a, with every choice of a ascribed to captivity. In a scan of 20 samples of this design one did (seed 9):

  • the outcome constants ran to about 10, with standard errors above 13;
  • the split constant of a fell to 0.34, with a standard error of 0.065, against its true value of 1.

That is the data’s own maximum: a refit from the true values reaches it, and one from the outcome constants raised by 5 returns to it. The fit raises no flag. Large outcome constants with larger standard errors are the sign. At such a fit the split coefficients’ small standard errors are the misleading part, and the bootstrap does not repair them: 200 refits give the split constant of a a standard error of 0.084, against the analytic 0.065, for an estimate 0.34 whose true value is 1, although they put the outcome constants’ standard errors above 300. Compare instead with the model that has fewer inflated alternatives, by boot_lr_test().

The model with fewer inflated alternatives is the boundary at which a captive share is zero, so boot_lr_test(imnl(y ~ x1 + x2 | z1, data = dc, inflate = "a"), mc) compares the two by simulation, as it compares the inflated model with the multinomial logit.

The split covariate here, z1, is not in the outcome equations. In the simulation reported in ?imnl, splitting on an outcome covariate instead left the intervals of that covariate’s outcome coefficients at 0.89-0.90 coverage with 5,000 cases and 0.80-0.81 with 2,000.

Links and boundaries

link = "probit" replaces the logistic split equation by a standard normal one (with one inflated alternative). When the split equation puts every case in one regime the inflated model collapses onto the multinomial logit, and with several inflated alternatives a captive share can collapse to zero; the fit then warns that it is at a boundary, and the standard errors of the split coefficients are not to be interpreted.

References

Bagozzi, B.E. and Marchetti, K. (2017). Distinguishing occasional abstention from routine indifference in models of vote choice. Political Science Research and Methods, 5(2), 277-294.

Campbell, D.E. and Monson, J.Q. (2008). The religion card: Gay marriage and the 2004 presidential election. Public Opinion Quarterly, 72, 399-419.

Gaudry, M.J.I. and Dagenais, M.G. (1979). The dogit model. Transportation Research Part B, 13, 105-111.

Swait, J. and Ben-Akiva, M. (1987). Empirical test of a constrained choice discrete model: Mode choice in Sao Paulo, Brazil. Transportation Research Part B, 21, 103-115.

Tse, Y.K. (1987). A diagnostic test for the multinomial logit model. Journal of Business and Economic Statistics, 5, 283-286.

Vuong, Q.H. (1989). Likelihood ratio tests for model selection and non-nested hypotheses. Econometrica, 57, 307-333.

Wilson, P. (2015). The misuse of the Vuong test for non-nested models to test for zero-inflation. Economics Letters, 127, 51-53.
